Empirical Research Plan: Mandated Maternity Benefits and Labor-Market Outcomes, CPS 1979-1989  

-------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Two-way fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID) with staggered adoption, supplemented by an event-study (Sun & Abraham, 2020) to uncover dynamic effects and to diagnose pre-trends.  
Why appropriate:  
• Policy adoption varies across states and over time → clear treated vs. untreated units.  
• CPS provides repeated cross-sections at the individual level → canonical setting for DID.  
• Event-study graphs allow visual/ statistical inspection of the parallel-trend assumption and estimation of time-since-treatment effects.  

-------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
• Treated observation = woman of child-bearing age (18–45) residing in a state s in year t in which a maternity-benefit mandate is in force.  
Control group / counterfactual  
• Primary: comparable women (18–45) in states that have not yet adopted the mandate in year t.  
• Secondary placebos: (i) Women aged 46–55 in all states, (ii) Men aged 18–45, to test for gender-specific shocks.  
Treatment timing  
• Adoption year = first calendar year mandate became binding in state-level statute. For staggered adopters, units switch once and remain treated.  
(No RDD; thus no running variable or cutoff.)  

-------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the mandate, outcomes for treated and control states would have evolved similarly for women 18–45.  
Plausibility: Mandate was often legislated for political, not macro-economic, reasons; still must be verified with pre-trend tests.  

A2. No anticipation: Employers and workers do not adjust outcomes before the effective date.  
Plausibility: Many mandates took effect quickly; nevertheless, propose to drop 1–2 leads in event study to test for anticipatory behavior.  

A3. Stable composition: Migration across states is not systematically linked to both treatment and outcomes.  
Plausibility: Short time window + limited evidence of migration driven solely by maternity insurance; but will test using CPS migration questions.  

A4. No spillovers: The policy in one state does not directly affect outcomes in control states.  
Plausibility: Some multi-state employers might internalize benefits nationwide; will check robustness by excluding multi-state firms’ intensive states (using industry*state shares).  

-------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

T1. Differential pre-trends  
• Mitigation: Event-study leads, state-specific linear trends, and trimming states that fail pre-trend F-tests.  

T2. Confounding contemporaneous policies (e.g., state-level parental-leave, minimum-wage changes)  
• Mitigation: Control vector of state-year covariates (minimum wage, unemployment rate, Medicaid expansions, etc.). Sensitivity analysis dropping states implementing major coincident reforms.  

T3. Selective migration/compositional change  
• Mitigation: Compare CPS migration question (moved within past year) and re-weight states by “stay-ers.” Show results unchanged when restricting to individuals present in the same state in t-1.  

-------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Required packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # modern TWFE and Sun-Abraham estimator
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
cps <- fread("cps_1979_1989.csv")   # assume annual March CPS extract

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
# keep prime sample
cps <- cps[age >= 18 & age <= 55]

# key demographics
cps[, female       := (sex == "Female")]
cps[, childbearing := female & age >= 18 & age <= 45]
cps[, older_women  := female & age >= 46 & age <= 55]
cps[, young_men    := !female & age >= 18 & age <= 45]

# Treatment timing matrix (manual or external file)
treat_dates <- fread("state_maternity_mandate_year.csv")  # state, adopt_year
cps <- merge(cps, treat_dates, by = "state")

# treatment status: 1 if mandate is in force in state-year
cps[, treat := as.integer(year >= adopt_year)]

# never-treated = 0, yet-to-treat = 0 before adopt_year
# Already satisfies Sun & Abraham requirements

# 3. DID main specification -----------------------------------------------
# Outcome example: employment (emp   =1 if employed)
cps[, emp := as.integer(lf_status == "Employed")]
# outcome example: log wages (lnw)
cps <- cps[emp == 1]                       # wage regression on employed only
cps[, lnw := log(earnings_hourly)]

# TWFE w/ state and year FE and covariates X
did_emp <- feols(emp ~ treat*childbearing +
                   state_unemp + min_wage +
                   educ + race + marital,
                 data = cps,
                 cluster = "state",
                 fe = ~ state + year)

did_wage <- feols(lnw ~ treat*childbearing +
                    state_unemp + min_wage +
                    educ + race + marital,
                  data = cps,
                  cluster = "state",
                  fe = ~ state + year)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham estimator) -------------------------------
cps[, rel_time := year - adopt_year]  # years relative to adoption
es <- feols(emp ~ sunab(adopt_year, year, ref.p = -1)*childbearing +
              state_unemp + min_wage + educ + race + marital,
            data = cps, cluster = "state", fe = ~ state + year)

iplot(es, ref.line = 0) + ggtitle("Event-study: Employment of child-bearing women")

# 5. Robustness: placebo sample (older women) -----------------------------
placebo <- feols(emp ~ treat*older_women +
                   state_unemp + min_wage + educ + race + marital,
                 data = cps, cluster = "state", fe = ~ state + year)

summary(placebo)
```

-------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  
Economic theory (benefit = non-wage labor cost) implies a small downward pressure on employment and/or cash wages for women most likely to use the benefit. Prior literature suggests effect sizes of –1 to –2 pp on employment rates and –1 % to –3 % on real hourly wages. Spillover to men or older women should be near zero.  

-------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1. Credible parallel pre-trends (visual & statistical): 0.8  
C2. Accurate treatment coding/timing: 1.0  
C3. No anticipatory behavior: 0.7  
C4. No spillovers/contamination: 0.6  
C5. No differential composition changes: 0.7  

(Scale: 1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable/absent)  

Overall, the strategy is strong but hinges on demonstrating parallel pre-trends and minimal cross-state spillovers.
